items.title: Iran is Reviewing ‘Concrete Proposals’ on Nuclear Program, Officials Say
items.summary: Iran’s willingness to re-engage on the issue suggests that Qatar-led diplomatic efforts to avert full-blown war between the U.S. and Iran have had some success.
items.full_text:
Title: Iran is Reviewing ‘Concrete Proposals’ on Nuclear Program, Officials Say - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/world/middleeast/peace-talks-iran-united-states-qatar-nuclear-program.html

Published Time: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:00:46 GMT

Markdown Content:
Iran is reviewing a set of proposals presented by mediators that could shape the future of its nuclear program, according to five officials briefed on the negotiations, representing a potential breakthrough in stalled diplomatic efforts to end its war with the United States.

Iran’s willingness to re-engage in nuclear talks, after weeks of refusing to budge, suggests recent mediation efforts led by Qatar to prevent a return to full-blown war have had some success, the officials said. They described the terms being reviewed as “concrete proposals,” without elaborating.

The Iranian foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The five officials, including an American and two Iranians, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details of the talks.

Qatar has spearheaded a diplomatic blitz with Iran in the past week, the officials added, participating in two rounds of talks in Tehran and hosting a third in Doha. Two of them said that the Qataris have also held recent talks with Iranian officials in Armenia.

Vice President JD Vance has emerged as a key proponent of the Qatari-led efforts to avert a military escalation, according to three of the officials. He has also appeared to try and distance himself from President Trump by [blaming the war](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/vance-iran-war-midterms-trump.html) for the Republicans’ heavy losses in the midterm elections this week.

Last month, Mr. Vance [sent a letter](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/us/politics/vance-peace-talks-letter-iran.html) to Mr. Rezaei proposing to hold direct peace talks that would also cover Iran’s nuclear program. Mr. Rezaei said the letter had shown that the United States had changed its tone toward Iran, which he described as a sign of the “Iranian nation’s strength and victory.”

Before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, Mr. Vance was the figure in Mr. Trump’s inner circle who was [most opposed to a full-scale war](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/07/us/politics/trump-iran-war.html). At the time, he warned Mr. Trump that a conflict could cause regional chaos and untold numbers of casualties.

On Monday, Mr. Vance [said progress](https://x.com/iclalturan/status/2117354206181179406) had been made with the Iranians, but he noted that Mr. Trump had both “kinetic” and “non-kinetic” options. “The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” he said.

The flurry of diplomacy comes as Mr. Trump and Israel have been weighing a large-scale attack against Iran. The American and Israeli militaries have[drawn up](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/us-israel-renewed-iran-strikes.html) a list of targets to strike, including energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy.

Iran’s nuclear program, which Mr. Trump says is an [effort to develop a bomb](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/07/us/politics/trump-iran-nuclear-promise.html) while the regime insists it is for peaceful purposes, has bedeviled efforts to find a long-term solution to end the war.

In June, the United States and Iran agreed to a [cease-fire](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/25/world/middleeast/us-iran-cease-fire-deal-violations.html). The deal was intended to pave the way for talks about the nuclear issue, and lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas shipments that Iran effectively closed early in the war. But the agreement collapsed, sparking months of intermittent clashes before the conflict settled into a tense stalemate.

Both Iran and the United States have used increasingly bellicose rhetoric in recent weeks, propelling Qatari mediators to try and broker a last-ditch deal between the two countries.

Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, suggested in a televised address on Saturday that Iran would not hold nuclear talks until the United States accepted the country’s demands. Those include releasing frozen Iranian assets, and lifting sanctions on the country’s oil and the U.S. naval blockade on Iran’s ports.

Privately, however, Mr. Rezaei has shown more openness to discussing the nuclear issue, according to the two Iranian officials and the American official. He has been negotiating with the Qataris alongside senior Iranian officials, including Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister, and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament.

The future of Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium has been one of the key sticking points in the talks. Mr. Trump has said Iran must give up the stockpile, which he has referred to as “nuclear dust.”

Iranian officials have been adamant that they will not ship the uranium outside the country. In previous rounds of talks, Iran has discussed [diluting the stockpile](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/world/middleeast/trump-iran-deal-obama.html) on its own soil under the supervision of international inspectors.

The International Atomic Energy Agency, the U.N. nuclear watchdog, estimated in a [report](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/gov2026-8.pdf) published this year that, as of June 2025, Iran had about 440 kilograms, or roughly 970 pounds, of highly enriched uranium. Experts say that it could be used to develop a small number of nuclear bombs.

As of Thursday morning, Iran and the United States were reviewing the latest suggestions from mediators to bridge any remaining gaps, two of the officials said.

Mr. Trump has vacillated between making bellicose threats to return to all-out war and saying he wants to give diplomacy a chance. On Wednesday, he said Mr. Vance’s assertion that the [war with Iran was to blame](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/vance-iran-war-midterms-trump.html) for the midterm defeat was “largely true,” but he also defended his decision to attack the country.

Oil prices fell sharply after the midterm results, as some observers thought it could encourage Mr. Trump to end the war.

Iranian leaders have warned that its forces would expand their range of targets if the country is attacked again. Senior Iranian officials and clerics are also debating whether Iran should [withdraw from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/europe/iran-nuclear-weapons-war.html?eafs_enabled=false), which prohibits the development of a nuclear weapon.

Gulf Arab officials have expressed [growing concerns](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/middleeast/trump-iran-war-midterms-election.html) that a renewed U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran could lead to [devastating retaliatory strikes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/world/middleeast/trump-iran-war-midterms-election.html?eafs_enabled=false) on their own countries, further straining their already bruised economies.

“From the perspective of the U.A.E., and I would also say Gulf countries, we don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” said Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates, at the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain over the weekend. “We want to see a diplomatic and political resolution of this protracted crisis.”

Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting to this article.

items.title: Lana Nusseibeh’s U.N. Bid Collides With U.A.E.’s Role in Sudan
items.summary: Lana Nusseibeh, one of the Gulf nation’s top diplomats, has led the effort to deny her country’s role in Sudan. Now it’s complicating her bid to become secretary general of the United Nations.
items.full_text:
Title: Lana Nusseibeh’s U.N. Bid Collides With U.A.E.’s Role in Sudan - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/world/africa/lana-nusseibeh-united-nations-uae-sudan.html

Published Time: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:59:07 GMT

Markdown Content:
The United Arab Emirates hired Colombian mercenaries to fight alongside a notorious Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide, United Nations investigators have found.

A confidential report submitted to the Security Council last week and obtained by The New York Times details how an Emirati security company with close ties to the government moved the Colombians into Sudan through territory controlled by Emirati proxies in Libya and Somalia.

The report is the most detailed accounting yet by the United Nations of the [Emirati role in Sudan’s civil war](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/21/world/africa/uae-sudan-civil-war.html), in which the Emirates is accused of supplying drones, weapons and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or R.S.F., fueling a conflict that has caused hundreds of thousands of deaths.

The U.N. findings come at a sensitive time for the Emirates. One of its top diplomats, Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, who for years has led Emirati efforts to deny her country’s role in Sudan, is a candidate to become the next secretary general of the United Nations.

Cambridge-educated and of Palestinian heritage, Ms. Nusseibeh, 48, has represented the Emirates at the United Nations for over a decade, returning in 2024 to the Emirates, where she was appointed minister of state for foreign affairs last year.

Since emerging in October as a last-minute candidate in the contest to lead the United Nations, Ms. Nusseibeh has shaken up the race while coming under sharp scrutiny for her role in Sudan. She is accused of trying to deny or downplay evidence that the Emirates, in violation of a U.N. arms embargo, has backed the R.S.F., a group accused of countless atrocities.

Image

Sudanese military forces beside an Emirati armored vehicle that had been captured from the Rapid Support Forces in the capital, Khartoum, last year. Credit...Ivor Prickett for The New York Times

Critics also say Ms. Nusseibeh has sought to silence, sometimes successfully, the work of U.N. bodies investigating Emirati policy in several Arab countries, where it has been accused of backing warlords and breaking international arms embargoes.

“Lana Nusseibeh has spent over a decade in roles acting for the U.A.E. government and repeatedly whitewashing their abusive role in Yemen and Sudan, presenting Abu Dhabi as a humanitarian actor while dismissing or obscuring mounting evidence of its role in fueling abuses,” [Bruno Stagno Ugarte](https://www.hrw.org/about/people/bruno-stagno-ugarte) of Human Rights Watch said in a statement.

Ms. Nusseibeh’s candidacy raised questions about whether she would be willing “to defend the independence and integrity of the U.N. and its investigative mechanisms, including those exposing U.A.E. abuses,” Mr. Ugarte said.

A spokesman for the Emirates denied the country supported any side in Sudan’s war or sought to undermine U.N. investigations. The Emirates separately told the U.N. that the security company named in the confidential report had not deployed mercenaries to Sudan or broken any Emirati law.

In an email, Ms. Nusseibeh said that ending the “terrible conflict” in Sudan would be her priority as secretary general. She pledged that if U.N. investigators identified a foreign power fueling the conflict, she would “act on it and engage that State.”

“Sudan will be a litmus test for the next Secretary-General,” she added.

Ms. Nusseibeh has been on the front lines of Emirati diplomacy on Sudan since the country fell into civil war in 2023.

Within months, the Emirates [began supplying weapons](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/09/29/world/africa/sudan-war-united-arab-emirates-chad.html), drones and military aid to the R.S.F., hoping to help the paramilitary group defeat Sudan’s military and assure Emirati interests in a country with deep gold deposits and a strategic position on the Red Sea. In 2024, The Times [revealed](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/21/world/africa/uae-sudan-civil-war.html) that the Emirates was flying powerful Chinese drones from a base in Chad, under the cover of a Red Cross operation.

Other countries and companies have fueled Sudan’s war as well, including Russia, Iran, Turkey and Ukraine, mostly by sending or selling weapons to Sudan’s military. But none have been as pivotal as the Emirates, which has used its vast resources and close alliances with countries like Ethiopia and Chad in support of the R.S.F.

In interviews, Ms. Nusseibeh has repeatedly said that her country is not backing the R.S.F. “Those allegations are categorically untrue,” she told CNN in 2024, adding that the Emirates sends only humanitarian aid to Sudan.

Image

Ms. Nusseibeh during an interview in Abu Dhabi, the Emirates, in March. She has denied that the Emirates is backing Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces.Credit...Abdelhadi Ramahi/Reuters

Behind closed doors, Ms. Nusseibeh has quietly pressed foreign allies to support the Emirati position of professed neutrality on Sudan, according to several former U.S. officials.

But even in private, she has refused to speak candidly about her country’s role in Sudan, complicating efforts to bring the conflict to a negotiated end, the officials added.

In 2024, Emirati leaders, angered that Britain had not defended them from attacks during a Security Council meeting on Sudan, canceled planned meetings with senior British ministers in retaliation, said a senior former U.S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive deliberations.

More recently, scrutiny of the Emirati role in Sudan has focused on the so-called Desert Wolves, a group of Colombian mercenaries hired to fight alongside the R.S.F. Several news outlets and rights groups have documented how the Colombians flew drones, trained fighters and provided artillery support as the R.S.F. carried out its punishing siege of the Sudanese city of El Fasher last year, one of the most notorious episodes of the war.

While the Emirates has often brushed past negative news reports, it appeared defensive earlier this year when the United Nations also accused the Emirates of providing Colombian mercenaries in Sudan.

In July, a panel of United Nations investigators monitoring an arms embargo on Darfur sent a detailed report to the Security Council that contained a blunt assertion: “The U.A.E. supported the R.S.F. by providing mercenaries,” it wrote.

Colombian mercenaries had been trained at two military bases in Abu Dhabi before being deployed to Sudan, it said. Emirati officials mounted a fierce pushback, and before the report could be made public it was blocked at the Security Council over objections from Bahrain, which currently holds a nonpermanent seat.

A senior U.N. official and a regional diplomat who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters said Bahrain had been acting at the behest of the Emirates.

The Emirates “rejects as unfounded the allegation it is influencing any Security Council member,” its spokesman said. Bahrain’s foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The investigators’ latest report, sent to the Security Council on Friday, said the mercenaries were hired by Global Security Services Group, an Abu Dhabi-based private security company with strong political, business and familial ties to senior figures in the Emirati ruling family.

Image

A damaged power station after a reported drone strike by the Rapid Support Forces north of Omdurman, Sudan, last week.Credit...Ebrahim Hamid/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Analysts say the growing scrutiny of Ms. Nusseibeh’s record on Sudan may be hurting her campaign for secretary general. A recent straw poll of eight candidates placed her in the middle of the field.

Cameron Hudson, a former C.I.A. analyst and director for African affairs at the National Security Council, said the continued Emirati denials of support to the R.S.F. “make a mockery” of the investigative mechanisms that Ms. Nusseibah now seeks to lead.

“She played a significant role in obfuscating her government’s contribution to atrocities in Sudan,” he said. “That ought to disqualify her from any further consideration.”

Under Ms. Nusseibah, the Emirates has sought to quell U.N. scrutiny of its actions in other countries, too.

In 2011, the Emirates, alongside Saudi Arabia, successfully lobbied to close down a panel of U.N. investigators reporting on rights violations and other abuses in Yemen, where Emirati troops were deployed.

In 2016, Ms. Nusseibah corresponded with other Emirati officials over U.N. accusations that their country was arming the warlord Khalifa Hifter in Libya. “The fact of the matter is that the U.A.E. violated the Security Council resolution on Libya and continues to do so,” one Emirati official wrote to Ms. Nusseibah in a chain of emails that were accidentally sent to the U.N.

The U.N. published several of the emails but redacted the name of the official. The Times obtained an unredacted copy of that correspondence this week, identifying the official as Ahmed al Qasimi, a diplomat who worked for Ms. Nusseibeh at the U.N. mission in New York.

In November 2025, Ms. Nusseibeh led a concerted Emirati effort to influence members of the European Parliament over a pending resolution condemning atrocities in Sudan, [Politico reported](https://www.politico.eu/article/uae-avoids-blame-sudan-war-atrocities-eu-parliament-text/). The Parliament [passed the resolution](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2025-0310_EN.html) without mentioning the Emirates.

items.title: Parents Sue Google Over A.I. Safety Risks on School Chromebooks
items.summary: A student made plans to end her life after chatting with Google’s artificial intelligence, a new lawsuit claims, amid mounting concerns about online harms to children.
items.full_text:
Title: Parents Sue Google Over A.I. Safety Risks on School Chromebooks - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/technology/ai-safety-school-chromebooks-google-lawsuit.html

Published Time: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 17:30:32 GMT

Markdown Content:
After chatting for months with Google’s artificial intelligence on a school-issued Chromebook laptop, a 13-year-old student made plans to end her life, according to a lawsuit filed in California Superior Court on Monday, the latest in a wave of litigation over Big Tech’s effects on young people.

The lawsuit, which calls the girl Emma, said her parents first learned she had access to Google’s A.I. in mid-March after her school sent a message warning she was in “imminent danger” of self-harm. Emma’s mother logged into the teen’s school Google account and found her daughter composing a suicide note on Google Docs, the complaint said. Her parents, called John and Jane Doe in the lawsuit, immediately took Emma for an emergency psychiatric evaluation. She now goes to therapy every week.

Emma, a seventh grader in Charlotte, N.C., had grown convinced she had multiple mental health disorders following interactions with A.I. Mode, a chatbot-like feature on Google Search, the complaint said. She also searched for “what is a suicide note,” and made comments like “I am planning my own funeral” to the A.I., the complaint said.

The lawsuit is likely the first to claim that Google “hastily integrated” A.I. features into company apps used on K-12 Chromebooks, Google-powered laptops provided to millions of children by U.S. school districts, while failing to notify parents of potential risks. The claims add to mounting public concern that Silicon Valley has hooked young people on social media apps, video games and A.I. chatbots, putting children in harm’s way.

José Castañeda, a Google spokesman, said the company had worked extensively with health experts to build features to help young people find emergency resources. The company is reviewing the claims in the lawsuit.

“For years, we’ve shown hotline information directly in search when someone may be experiencing a mental health crisis,” he said in a statement. “We’ve built those same protections into search A.I. features, connecting people with real-world support.”

The case underscores how public school districts have come to depend on classroom laptops, tablets and apps from companies like Google and Microsoft. In recent years, some Big Tech companies have used their own infrastructure in schools to promote their A.I. chatbots for teachers and students.

The new lawsuit argues that Google’s “sprawling digital ecosystem” of laptops and apps has enabled the tech giant to spread its Gemini A.I. chatbot across public schools — as well as [turn on some students’ access to A.I. features by default](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/14/business/google-gemini-ai-schools.html) — without parents’ awareness or permission. While school administrators can toggle company apps like YouTube and Gemini on or off for students in different grades, school administrators have complained that Google’s system has not allowed them to disable A.I. Mode and A.I. Overview, features embedded in Google Search.

This week, Google said that it planned to automatically turn off certain A.I. apps and features — including its Gemini A.I. tool and search — in K-12 schools in early 2027. Schools that elect to turn search back on will have a choice: to enable student access to the A.I. features that the company has already embedded in search; or to a new A.I. feature intended to assist students with schoolwork. Google is not offering schools an option to turn off A.I. in search, a company executive said, because “[search and A.I. are deeply integrated](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html).”

Image

Google said this week that it planned to turn off certain A.I. services in K-12 schools in early 2027.Credit...David Robert Elliott for The New York Times

Big Tech has faced a wave of litigation this year over technology’s effects on young users. Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, recently agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to settle charges from 47 states that it used [addictive features to ensnare children](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/technology/meta-settlement-social-media-addiction-lawsuit.html?eafs_enabled=false), following [losses in similar cases](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/06/technology/meta-new-mexico-child-safety.html). Meta has denied wrongdoing. Several parents have also sued A.I. companies over allegations their children died by suicide following interactions with chatbots.

The lawsuit filed on Monday on behalf of Emma and her parents makes arguments similar to some recently used against Meta, claiming that Emma was harmed by Google’s products.

Emma, who had limited access to laptops and apps at home, did not initially try to use Google’s A.I. on her school-issued device, according to the complaint. As Emma searched the web, the lawsuit claimed, Google “routed” her to its A.I. Mode, a chatbot-like feature on Google Search.

By March Emma was “exchanging thousands of messages” with Google’s A.I. Mode until late into the night and “resumed as soon as she woke up,” according to the complaint. The A.I. “diagnosed Emma with major mental illnesses, persuaded her to trust it over her parents and counselors, and ultimately helped her plan her suicide and funeral,” the complaint said.

Google’s product system did not alert the school or Emma’s parents that her searches and A.I. chats suggested she was at risk of harming herself, according to the complaint. Her school used a digital monitoring company, which automatically scans students’ writing and searches on school devices for signs of self-harm, cyberbullying and other problems.

In an interview last month, Emma’s parents said that they learned she was in crisis only after the monitoring company flagged a suicide plan she was writing in Google Docs and warned her school.
